articles.title: Joseph Kabila: DR Congo ex-president named leader of new M23 rebel coalition
articles.summary: Joseph Kabila had previously denied having links to the M23 rebels, which control much of eastern DR Congo.
articles.body:
Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named the leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government.

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it aimed to coordinate "resistance forces" to end "tyranny" in Democratic Republic of Congo and would pursue the goal "by all means, including force".

Its unveiling on Monday is the clearest indication so far of Kabila's direct involvement in an armed movement a year after he was sentenced to death in absentia for treason. He had previously denied having links to the M23 rebel group.

The Congolese government has not commented.

Claude Ibalanky, the coalition's adviser, announced the group's leadership at a press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the largest city in eastern DR Congo, which has been under the control of the M23 since last year.

Video released by the group showed Kabila signing documents at the group's declaration along with other leaders.

M23 leader Sultani Makenga will serve as one of Kabila's four deputies in the new movement. The other three also come from the AFC-M23 alliance which last year seized much of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo.

What's the fighting in DR Congo all about?

The announcement of the new group comes days after Kabila delivered an address in which he said he would set out how Congolese people should act to "rescue" their country.

On Friday, Kabila accused President Félix Tshisekedi's government of disregarding proposals he had put forward last year, including some aimed at ending the conflict in eastern DR Congo.

Kabila also accused the government of undermining constitutional rule, mismanaging the economy and failing to improve security. He further alleged arbitrary arrests of political opponents and military officers.

The government has not publicly responded to those claims.

Kabila, 55, ruled DR Congo from 2001 until January 2019, when Tshisekedi took office following a disputed election.

The two were once political allies, forming an informal power-sharing arrangement after the transfer of power. They later fell out and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in 2023 before returning to Goma last year.

The former president had remained largely out of public view for several years but has become increasingly critical of his successor's administration.

The formation of the new coalition comes at an uncertain time in a country that has been wracked by violence for decades.

More than 100 militia groups are active in eastern DR Congo amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources.

The UN and Western governments accuse Rwanda of backing the M23 and controlling the rebels.

Rwanda denies supporting the M23 despite overwhelming evidence, and says its military presence in eastern DR Congo is a defensive measure against threats posed by Congolese armed groups.

Tshisekedi's second term ends in 2028 but in May he said that elections, which are due then, may not be held because of the conflict.

He also hinted that he may seek re-election for a third term "if the people want".

The parliament has since passed a bill that could pave the way for a referendum that could remove the constitution's two-term limit.

Last month, authorities clashed with protesters holding demonstrations in the capital against the proposed changes.

Richard Moncrieff, who monitors Africa's Great Lakes region for the International Crisis Group (ICG) says the new coalition is aimed at trying to enlarge the rebellion.

He argues that through his "higher profile", Kabila hopes to get support from people dissatisfied with Tshisekedi "beyond the very narrow political base that the M23 enjoys".

The analyst says this appears to be Kabila's objective, to draw more senior Congolese army officers to his side and "lessen the reliance of the M23 on its Rwandan backers".

Kabila came to power after the assassination of his father Laurent Kabila, who headed a national rebellion in the 1990s, backed by Rwanda. His forces marched across the country, starting in the east, before taking over in the capital Kinshasa, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) away.

Moncrieff says Kabila is drawing on that past to proclaim the illegitimacy of Tshisekedi's government.

He however says it won't be easy to seize power like his father, partly because the US has imposed sanctions on Kabila, which he says presumes American support for DR Congo's government.

In May the US imposed sweeping sanctions on Kabila, accusing him of backing the M23, providing financial support, encouraging defections from the Congolese army. Kabila said the measures were unjustified and politically motivated.

The US said they were part of a wider effort to support last year's peace deal between DR Congo and Rwanda that it brokered.

The latest events show peace negotiations are "going nowhere and attempting to gain control on the ground is the priority for all parties," the ICG analyst says.

articles.title: Former DR Congo President Kabila joins M23 rebels in a new coalition
articles.summary: Alliance raises fears of more fighting and confrontation with President Tshisekedi’s government.
articles.body:
Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has launched a new political and military coalition, including the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group, which has captured vast areas of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Kabila introduced the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) at a news conference on Monday at his residence in the eastern city of Goma, which the M23 has controlled since January 2025.

Kabila said he will head the FRN with rebel leaders, including Corneille Nangaa , the former leader of the Congo River Alliance (AFC) and the political wing of M23, serving as his deputies.

Claude Ibalanky, a coalition adviser, said the group aims to unite all resistance forces “to put an end to tyranny by any means necessary, including the use of force”.

There was no immediate response to the announcement from the DRC government.

Reporting from Goma, Al Jazeera’s Alain Uaykani said there were growing fears that fighting in eastern DRC could escalate.

“Kabila addressed the nation, explaining his plan. People are making comments across the country that this is another level of the conflict,” Uaykani explained.

Uaykani said rebels already hold Goma, Bukabu, the airports and key border crossings with Rwanda and Uganda, and that the government has been unable to push them back. Talks to resolve the conflict have also failed, with each side blaming the other.

“The government has shown no sign of defeating these people,” he said.

Uaykani noted that Kabila is a former army chief and said there were fears that government troops could defect.

“He’s still a soldier; he has led an army. People are worried that more soldiers from the government may join him as well”.

Yvon Muya, a researcher at the University of Ottawa in Canada, said the announcement increases the chances of a confrontation between Kabila and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi, and could lead to more fighting in eastern DRC.

“You don’t make an announcement like this without having prepared the actions that follow,” Muya said. “We will likely witness an escalation on the military front.”

Representatives from the DRC government and the M23 movement were expected to meet in Qatar in November for talks, but analysts warn that the new coalition could undermine the process.

Kabila led the DRC from 2001 to 2019, taking office at 29 after his father, President Laurent Kabila, was assassinated.

A DRC military court sentenced Joseph Kabila to death in absentia last year on charges of treason, war crimes and crimes against humanity, finding that he collaborated with Rwanda and M23.

Kabila has called the case politically motivated and denies the charges.

The US imposed sanctions on him earlier this year over his alleged role in funding rebel groups.

The DRC, the United States and United Nations experts accuse Rwanda of backing M23, an allegation Rwanda denies.

Tshisekedi’s second term ends in 2028, and his allies have been preparing public opinion for changes to the constitution’s two-term limit, as rebel activities intensify in the east.

articles.title: Israeli forces raid Palestinian NGOs in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Snipers deployed outside entrances to the Palestine Medical Complex, Wafa reported.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have raided the offices of two Palestinian nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) and the courtyard of the Palestine Medical Complex in the occupied West Bank.

Israeli forces searched the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees and the Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association in the city of Ramallah on Tuesday.

Israeli snipers were also deployed around the entrances to the Palestine Medical Complex in Ramallah, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

The hospital is the largest government medical facility in the West Bank.

Reporting from Ramallah, Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim said Israeli forces were confiscating equipment belonging to Addameer, an NGO that focuses on prisoner rights.

“Israeli forces have been raiding one of the compounds that belong to Addameer. The NGO has been closed before by the Israeli forces. It has been deemed by the Israeli army and establishment as a terrorist organisation,” Ibrahim said.

“This is a daylight raid that is happening in the centre of Ramallah, causing a lot of panic. Palestinians [currently] have children at school. Others have [relatives] at work. People are worried because they know Israeli forces can open fire on them. Earlier, that happened: Israeli forces fired stun grenades at journalists covering this raid.”

Al Jazeera Arabic also reported that a journalist was injured after Israeli forces fired tear gas during the attacks. Israeli forces detained another four journalists in Hebron, according to Wafa. Photojournalists Hazem Badr, Musa Qawasmi, Musab Shawar, and Mamoun Wazwaz were detained east of Idnha town and blocked from completing their reporting assignments.

The Palestinian Ministry of Health reported that a child was injured by Israeli live ammunition and several others had suffered from suffocation due to the ongoing raids in Ramallah and el-Bireh.

The raid on the NGOs is the latest act in an Israeli campaign of aggression against Palestinian civil society organisations.

In 2021, Israel designated six Palestinian organisations, including Addameer and the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees, as “terrorist” organisations.

At the time, the Israeli Ministry of Defence claimed that the organisations used activism as a cover but “in practice belong and constitute an arm of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the main activity of which is the ‘liberation of Palestine’ and destruction of Israel”.

Founded in 1991, Addameer works to support Palestinian prisoners held in Israeli and Palestinian prisons, offering free legal aid and advocating their rights at the national and international level, according to its mission statement.

The Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees was founded in 1980 to empower Palestinian women on all levels and to “contribute to the Palestinian national struggle against the Israeli military’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories”, according to its Facebook page.

articles.title: Traditional two-parent families vanish from big American cities as 'marriage deserts' expand
articles.summary: A new report from the Institute for Family Studies reveals a 70-point divide in traditional two-parent families, as urban marriage deserts expand across major U.S. cities.
articles.body: The traditional two-parent nuclear family is far less common in parts of major American cities than in suburban communities, with fewer than a quarter of households with children headed by married couples in some neighborhoods in Cleveland, Washington, D.C., Milwaukee and Detroit, according to a new report. The study from the Institute for Family Studies showed that the share of households with children headed by married couples varies by roughly 70 percentage points across the areas studied, highlighting a divide between urban "married-family deserts" and suburban "married-family gardens." The findings revealed differences in family structure across the country, raising questions about how the neighborhoods where children grow up may influence their opportunities for upward mobility. DRIVEN BY PROGRESSIVE DOOMISM, LIBERALS ARE HAVING FEWER BABIES THAN CONSERVATIVE FAMILIES "Marriage and raising kids are both parts of your life that really force you to kind of die to yourself and live for others," Ken Burchfiel, a research fellow at the Institute for Family Studies, told Fox News Digital. "When you have lots of parents, lots of husbands and wives in a region, I imagine just overall the cultural focus is less on 'how can I get ahead in life' and more on 'what can I do for my family?’" The study analyzed 2020 Census data to identify where married and married-parent households are most and least common. It found that suburban neighborhoods tend to have higher marriage rates, while major urban centers often have lower rates. NORTH TEXAS DOMINATES IN POPULATION GROWTH AS BIG BLUE CITIES FAIL TO RECOVER TO PRE-PANDEMIC LEVELS Suburban Dallas-Fort Worth stands as the nation's largest grouped "marriage garden," while Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn form the largest grouped "marriage desert," covering nearly 686,000 householders, more than two-thirds of whom are unmarried. "This does not appear to describe small variations around shared national norms, but rather two distinct family-formation regimes, so stark it could even be described as family structure polarization," the IFS report stated. Burchfiel said high incomes do not necessarily translate into higher marriage rates either. In high-income Manhattan neighborhoods, including the Financial District and Greenwich Village, fewer than 28% of householders ages 15 to 64 are married. GEN Z IS WORKING HARD, BUT THE ECONOMY IS PUTTING THE AMERICAN DREAM OUT OF REACH FOR MANY "It’s clear that the decision to get married is not just due to financial concerns; it's also a matter of culture and, admittedly, perhaps a matter of affordability," Burchfiel said. "I recognize, having lived in New York for a few years, that having a high salary does not mean that it's easy to buy a house, raise a family. It can still be extremely difficult and probably many of the people in those areas who do get married find themselves moving out to the suburbs," he added. The IFS researchers said they examined the issue because of a large body of research showing that "family structure is closely associated with economic mobility and broader measures of social capital." They pointed to research by Harvard economist Raj Chetty that found the share of homes with two parents present was the strongest predictor of upward mobility in a community. "This represents a significant discrepancy in lived experience for children growing up in these distinct environments. Those in married-family gardens grow up with married parents, in neighborhoods, schools and after-school activities where most peers experience the same. These children will be observing marriage as a stable, ordinary feature of adult life," the study explained. US HURTLING TOWARD POPULATION DECLINE EVEN AS AMERICANS SAY THEY WANT BIGGER FAMILIES, NEW REPORT WARNS "By contrast, for children in married-family deserts, there is likely to be much greater churn in adult relationship stability, and greater inconsistency in supervision, where marriage and stable relationship bonds are atypical or distant from everyday norms — both for these children and their peers." Areas with some of the lowest shares of married-parent households nationwide included eastern Cleveland and nearby Bratenahl Village, Ohio, with only 18% of households with children headed by a married couple, followed closely by eastern Washington, D.C., at 20% and central Milwaukee at 22%. In suburban "married-family gardens" like Fremont City, California, Lakewood, New Jersey and parts of Utah County, Utah, up to 89% of households with children are headed by married couples. Burchfiel advised newlyweds and young couples evaluating where to settle down to look closely at these family maps alongside local job markets, but to also take into account their own personal circumstances, such as staying close to extended family. THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH "Living near other married couples can be really useful when you're settling down and raising a family," Burchfiel said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's worth seeing where those married couples are and where maybe they're avoiding, because again, if there's an area where 70-plus percent of individuals are married, that's probably a good place to settle down as a married couple," he added.

articles.title: German airport briefly shuts after ‘emergency code’ transmitted in error by incoming plane
articles.summary: Germany’s Nuremberg airport temporarily suspended flights on Tuesday after an emergency code was transmitted in error by an incoming plane due to a “brief malfunction.”
articles.body: Germany’s Nuremberg airport temporarily suspended flights on Tuesday after an emergency code was transmitted in error by an incoming plane due to a “brief malfunction.” Corendon Airlines said a flight from the Greek island of Corfu to Nuremberg, southern Germany, sent out the alert “while in Croatian airspace due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system.” “The situation was immediately monitored, investigations were promptly initiated and all necessary preparations were made,” the airline told CNN. Earlier on Tuesday, Nuremberg airport said flight operations had been suspended “for the time being” due to the incident. In its statement, the airport referred to a flight from Corfu to Nuremberg, which it said “landed safely.” Flight operations at the airport have since returned to normal, Reuters reported. Local police told CNN there is no danger and everyone on board is safe. Shortly after 11 a.m. local time an emergency report was received from within the cockpit of the plane, police said. They added that the flight was escorted into Nuremberg airport by Eurofighter jets. “The aircraft in question is a scheduled flight from Corfu, which landed in Nuremberg as planned. On-site inspections have determined that there is no danger,” police posted on X. German newspaper Bild reported previously that a possible drone sighting had disrupted air traffic at the airport overnight into Tuesday, with three pilots independently reporting an object they had seen during takeoff or landing. Police later told CNN the incident on Tuesday was not related to any possible drone sightings. This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday reiterated that the Union territory of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday reiterated that the Union territory of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India. The ministry said that no amount of denial by the Chinese side can change this established fact. The statement came after a statement by the Chinese foreign ministry opposed the naming of certain strategic locations in Ladakh.Rejecting the claims, the MEA said: "The announcement mentions that the twenty-eight (28) places/features located in the UT of Ladakh have been identified with standard place and feature names on the official map of Survey of India, and it has been done in consultation with the Union Territory of Ladakh and local stakeholders. Identifying these places formally on the Survey of India map of UT of Ladakh is aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large."On 2 October, India formally identified 28 strategic locations and geographical features in Ladakh on its official map, including key border friction points along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), such as Gogra and Hot Spring. The move, undertaken in consultation with the Ladakh administration, aimedto improve official mapping, ensure precise identification and raise public awareness of the sensitive border region.Gogra and Hot Spring were among the friction points during the 2020 standoff between Indian and Chinese troops and remain important for patrolling along the LAC. The standoff began on 5 May 2020 after a clash near Pangong Lake. Disengagement efforts began in 2022. articles.title: Regime change in Iran is needed now more than ever
articles.summary: Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy and Imperial Japan taught the Greatest Generation in the 1930s and 1940s the painful lesson that pure evil does exist on a grand scale in the contemporary world. It took the global horrors and sacrifices of the Second World War to end the ravages of those depraved regimes. Immediately after the…
articles.body:
Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy and Imperial Japan taught the Greatest Generation in the 1930s and 1940s the painful lesson that pure evil does exist on a grand scale in the contemporary world. It took the global horrors and sacrifices of the Second World War to end the ravages of those depraved regimes. Immediately after the war, the Soviet Union and its proxies and allies took up where the defeated Axis powers had left off in the pursuit of world domination under a totalitarian international order.

Despite the emergence of the new global threat, the advent of nuclear weapons made a third world war — a civilizational conflict — increasingly immoral and unthinkable among Western societies. The Soviet Union, by contrast, frequently brandished its atomic weapons to deter Western intervention as it spread communist power and ideology to vulnerable societies in Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas.

Belatedly aroused to the dangers of global communist expansion in the postwar period, the Truman administration responded in January 1950 by dispatching Secretary of State Dean Acheson to deliver remarks on U.S. national security interests in Asia. Acheson traced a security perimeter across the region ; unfortunately, it did not include either Taiwan or South Korea as critical U.S. security interests.

Josef Stalin, Mao Zedong and Kim Il Sung conferred on whether Taiwan or South Korea should be the next target of communist expansion. Kim won the argument — or rather, preempted it — in June 1950, by unleashing a massive invasion of South Korea across the 38th Parallel. The invading Northern forces were soon joined by hundreds of thousands of Chinese Communist ground troops, supported by Soviet arms and economic assistance.

Truman, now fully awakened to the immediate danger, responded by mobilizing a United Nations “police action”, so named to avoid any suggestion that the world was returning to the global conflict that had engulfed it just five years earlier. That meant that “unconditional surrender” and “regime change” were excluded from the vocabulary and strategic planning options of the U.S. and its allies. The Korean War thus set the precedent of “limited war,” in which horizontal escalation against the major powers arming and sustaining aggressive lesser powers was taken off the table.

The aggressor nations, while thwarted in their immediate expansionist efforts, were left to fight another day.

Today, three-quarters of a century after the end of the Korean War, North Korea remains part of the original “axis of evil” that President George W. Bush identified in 2002 as comprising Iran, Iraq and North Korea. With Russia and China having openly declared their “comprehensive strategic partnerships” with Iran, alongside their longstanding alliance with North Korea and each other, the quadripartite collusion constitutes a far more powerful and dangerous axis of evil menacing the West today.

Western powers now confront three possible approaches to the new challenge presently led by Iran.

The U.S. and the West can continue on their existing course with a combination of negotiations, economic pressures, and occasional limited military forays against Teheran’s renewed efforts to acquire a nuclear weapon and the means to deliver it to a Western target. But such a response by the U.S. and its allies would perpetuate the economically and politically draining on again, off again kinetic confrontation between Iran and the West. Americans have no tolerance for another strategic stalemate or “forever war,” especially after President Trump’s erratic mishandling of the first six months of the current conflict.

Alternatively, Trump can deal with Iran, openly or furtively, by capitulating to its effective control of the Gulf of Hormuz . But that would establish a devastating abandonment of the centuries-old global freedom of navigation principle. What’s more, it would all but guarantee a major war in the Taiwan Strait, as China, supported militarily and materially by Russia, North Korea and Iran, would very likely seek to exploit the rending of the maritime order by asserting its longtime claim on Taiwan. Trump or his immediate successor would be compelled to respond militarily, or to concede the strategic defeat of the U.S. — the ultimate betrayal of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.

The third possible U.S. response to the existential Iran threat is to return to Trump’s original, seemingly instinctive approach: that the Islamic Republic is entirely irredeemable in its pursuit of nuclear weapons, its regional and global terrorism campaign, and its brutal suppression of the Iranian people. Like the unreformable enemies of World War II and, more recently, the Saddam Hussein regime in Iraq , the Islamic Republic must be permanently eliminated from power.

Hopefully, Trump will have learned from the failure of his earlier attempt to change the Iranian regime that it will take more than an off-the-cuff, throw-away line appealing for unarmed Iranians to “take over your institutions.” That will require the kind of strategic communications that helped win the Cold War. Resuscitated institutions like Voice of America, the U.S. Information Agency and their sister news outlets all over the world can provide the people of Iran and the Mideast with sorely needed information denied to populations in closed societies for obvious reasons.

The mere announcement of such a multi-dimensional, partially kinetic campaign to change the regime, seriously led, coordinated and funded with material support, can ignite the motivation that will encourage defections from regime and military personnel. Once those elements refuse orders to suppress and murder their fellow Iranians, the end of the regime will be near.

Partisan and resistance forces in France, Italy, Poland and other oppressed populations in Eastern and Western Europe helped the Allies throw off the yoke of totalitarian oppression in World War II. On a smaller military scale, but with a much greater domestic uprising already proven to be available if modestly armed by Western supporters and defecting regime elements, Iran can soon rid itself of its oppressors and join the modern, civilized world.

Trump, perhaps the unlikeliest person to lead a moral cause, could partially redeem his disgraceful siding with Vladimir Putin’s criminal aggression against Ukraine . If, instead, he continues his fascination with Russia’s murderous tyrant, he will soon have to deal with another aggressor — his “friend” Xi Jinping when China attacks Taiwan, its own small democratic neighbor. History will judge Trump harshly for his failure to recognize the danger, just as Neville Chamberlain did with Hitler, and Truman and Acheson did with Kim Il Sung.

He is a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Corean-American Studies, a member of the advisory board of the Global Taiwan Institute and member of the advisory board of the Vandenberg Coalition.

articles.body: The United Kingdom has entered a new phase of national security as a “more contested era” replaces the stability of the post Cold War years, the head of the domestic security service MI5 said Tuesday, warning that threats from states and terrorists could be supercharged by artificial intelligence. Ken McCallum called on Britain to be more resilient and vigilant, warning that the country faces a “new era of national security” as it fends off hybrid threats from a triumvirate of hostile foreign states – Russia, Iran and China. “These days our terrorism and state threats operational missions are pretty much of equal scale; that in itself is a huge shift across recent years,” he said in his annual speech outlining threats facing the UK. Those threats can take many forms, including “arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, coercion (and) violence,” McCallum said. AI is “already supercharging” some of these threats, especially in cybersecurity, McCallum said as he announced the creation of a new AI Threat Assessment Center. The technology could also strengthen the capabilities of “comparatively low sophistication actors” if governments don’t place sufficient “guardrails” around it,” he warned. Most worryingly, AI has the potential to help make destructive bioweapons, though this has not yet been realized, he added. McCallum emphasized – echoing warnings from previous years – that the threat posed by states is now a key focus for the service. “You might be surprised to know that in 2026, MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War,” he said. “Over the last decade, our state threats caseload has quadrupled.” He warned the new heightened threat environment was not a “temporary blip.” Of these states, “Russia remains aggressor number one,” McCallum said, pointing to Moscow’s escalating campaign of “hybrid warfare” targeting European countries. He gave as examples a cyber attack on Polish energy infrastructure and an attempt to “use an explosive-laden drone to destroy a cargo plane in Germany.” In the UK, “a man was charged last month under the National Security Act for allegedly preparing to sabotage a drone factory in Swindon,” McCallum added. Still, these are not “the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand,” McCallum said, noting that Russia’s capacity for espionage has been greatly weakened since more than 1,000 of its foreign staff have been expelled from their host countries since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Instead, Russia has scrambled “to pay criminals to do their bidding,” McCallum said. Iran has used similar methods in an attempt to “expand their hybrid campaign,” he added. More than 50 people have been arrested in connection with Iran-linked plots, mostly directed against British Jewish communities, he said. McCallum also referenced “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites,” alluding to the incident at RAF Fairford last month. He refused to provide further detail due to ongoing investigations but called the Fairford incident “not unique.” “There have been other examples, not just in the UK, but around the world,” he added. Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was “almost certainly” responsible for directing a suspected plot to target the UK airbase used by US forces. Several senior Iranian officials have vehemently denied these accusations. Several men, including a British-Iranian dual national, were arrested in connection with the plot before being released on bail. Shortly after the incident, the US made the unusual decision to move all its long-range bombers stationed in the UK back to their home bases on American soil following an unspecified new threat. McCallum also accused China of conducting espionage in the UK, referencing an alert MI5 issued to the academic community two weeks ago and a case earlier this year which yielded the “first ever convictions for national security offences” connected to Beijing. While he emphasized the increasing role of states, he noted that terrorism “remains a top concern for MI5” and that an “attack is highly likely.”

articles.title: Christopher Lloyd’s former 1920s Hollywood bungalow was bought by Diva Zappa for $2.55 million in 2022; after extensive repairs and restoration, the revived compound sold for $2.82 million in just 12 days
articles.summary: Some houses are built to impress, while others tell a story that unfolds room by room.
articles.body: Some houses are built to impress, while others tell a story that unfolds room by room. In Los Angeles, a Spanish-style bungalow once owned by Back to the Future star Christopher Lloyd belongs firmly to the latter category. Blending Mediterranean influences, playful architectural details and traces of Hollywood history, the property has evolved from a modest 1920s residence into an unconventional compound. Artist Diva Zappa bought the home for $2.55 million in 2022 and undertook an extensive restoration before selling it for $2.82 million after just 12 days on the market, states an online report by Homes.A bungalow with a Hollywood pastAccording to Home, when Lloyd acquired the property in the 1980s, the original Spanish bungalow was a relatively modest two-bedroom, two-bathroom home. With architect Robert DeYoung, the actor expanded it into a more elaborate estate, adding a one-bedroom, one-bathroom guesthouse and transforming the outdoor space with a swimming pool and extensive hardscaping.The result was a distinctive mix of architectural influences, with adobe-inspired elements and flowing lines reminiscent of the work of Spanish architect Antoni Gaudí. Rather than following a single design language, the property embraced an eclectic character that reflected Lloyd’s creativity and sense of humour.Some of its most unusual details were personal. According to Homes, a mould of the actor’s face adorned the exterior of the guesthouse, while a light switch incorporated a prop from the Jules Verne Time Train featured in Back to the Future Part III. These touches gave the residence a personality rarely found in conventional luxury real estate. Across the main house and guesthouse, the compound offers more than 3,400 square feet of living space, adds the online report.An artist’s approach to restorationWhen Zappa discovered the property in 2022, its individuality remained intact, but years of insufficient maintenance had left it in need of considerable work. The artist saw potential in its unconventional design and took on the challenge of restoring it without erasing its history.Between 2023 and 2025, the renovation involved substantial structural and cosmetic improvements. New roofs were installed, countertops replaced and bathrooms renovated. The house was also raised so that a new foundation could be poured, with hand-laid crystals incorporated into the foundation as a personal, symbolic gesture, states the online report.The fireplaces received particular attention. Four were restored, while the fifth was completely replaced. Throughout the process, the aim was to preserve the original Spanish character and the architectural personality Lloyd had introduced, while making the property more comfortable for contemporary living. The restoration effectively gave the ageing compound a new lease of life without stripping away the details that made it distinctive.A distinctive home finds its buyerThe property’s sale comes amid a more measured Los Angeles housing market, where increased listings have given buyers greater choice and reduced the urgency that characterised earlier years. Homes that require extensive work or appeal to a specific audience can face a more challenging path to a sale. Yet Lloyd’s former residence proved an exception. After just one weekend of open houses, the property attracted enough interest to prompt a deadline for offers. It ultimately sold for $2.82 million, a $270,000 increase over Zappa’s 2022 purchase price.The swift sale underlines the appeal of homes with a strong sense of identity, particularly when their unusual features are supported by thoughtful restoration. In a market filled with polished, contemporary interiors, the Hollywood compound offered something harder to replicate: a layered architectural history, personal touches and a connection to one of cinema’s most recognisable franchises.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and Google MapsReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Character.AI files for bankruptcy, to sell some assets to Disney for $20 million
articles.summary: Chatbot platform Character.AI said on Monday it has filed for bankruptcy in the US and has agreed to sell some assets for $20 million to Walt Disney.
articles.body: Chatbot platform Character.AI said on Monday it has filed for bankruptcy in the US and has agreed to sell some assets for $20 million to Walt Disney. The generative AI platform has faced mounting legal challenges over its chatbots. Earlier this year, Character.AI and Alphabet’s Google settled a lawsuit by the mother of a 14-year-old Florida boy who killed himself after the startup’s chatbot allegedly encouraged him to do so. Kentucky has sued the company, saying its chatbots encouraged users to cut, starve or kill themselves, while Pennsylvania filed a lawsuit alleging its chatbots posed as doctors. According to Character.AI‘s proposal, Disney will be a “stalking-horse” bidder — an initial prospective buyer — for a non-exclusive perpetual license to some intellectual property. Other bidders can top Disney’s offer. Character.AI expects to close the sale of all its assets by late November or early December. Character Technologies, its US-based owner, listed estimated assets and liabilities of between $50 million and $100 million, according to a court filing. Disney will help the platform in the transition, using staff it has hired from Character.AI. The platform’s services would continue meanwhile, but would be shut down if it can’t find a buyer, the company said. Two former Google employees founded Character.AI in 2021. In 2024, Google licensed its technology and rehired the founders. The Financial Times reported in May 2024 that Meta and Elon Musk’s xAI were competing to partner with Character.AI. In July 2024, Musk denied a media report that xAI was considering buying the company. In September 2025, Disney sent Character.AI a cease-and-desist letter, demanding it stop using Disney’s copyrighted characters without permission. Character.AI said it had removed them.

articles.title: Deadly Houthi attacks in Yemen’s Taiz as government forces advance in Marib
articles.summary: Government forces engage in intense clashes as Houthi shelling targets residential areas and hospitals in Taiz.
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces say they have made strategic advances into the Marib governorate in north-central Yemen as they push on with operation “Dawn of Yemen”.

The offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, launched just over a week ago, comes after major gains by the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, in September, when it swept along the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said operation Dawn of Yemen aimed to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started.

Meanwhile, intense clashes and Houthi shelling on residential neighbourhoods in Taiz in the southwest of the country have caused dozens of civilian casualties.

In the northwest of Marib governorate, a military source told Al Jazeera that government troops have successfully taken control of strategic, commanding heights surrounding the strategic Maas camp facility in the Medghal district. The source noted this followed intensive attacks that had breached the Houthi group’s fortifications.

On the southern front, forces from the Saba and Bayhan axes announced the capture of the al-Muqailat and Jabal Zajjar positions north of the Harib district. Government forces claimed the fierce clashes resulted in the Houthis retreating and suffering human and material losses.

This field progress coincided with continued violent battles along the front lines in the north and south of Marib. Government forces launched concentrated strikes using warplanes, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements.

The armed forces’ media centre published footage it said documented drone attacks on Houthi military barracks and vehicles within the scope of the third military region’s operations, noting the destruction of multiple combat vehicles and equipment.

Above: Footage from the battles within the operational theatre of the seventh military region north of Marib: Media centre of armed forces.

Military spokesperson Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili announced on Monday that operations have involved 1,879 precise strikes, neutralising 950 Houthi fighters and destroying 380 military vehicles.

Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that air strikes targeted Kamaran Island and the al-Qanawis district in the coastal Hodeidah governorate along the Red Sea and the Harf Sufyan district in Amran, western-central Yemen.

In the southwestern governorate of Taiz, where the Houthis have the city of Taiz under siege , government forces and popular resistance fighters are engaged in fierce battles across multiple major axes amid a wide-scale field escalation.

On the western fronts, heavy fighting has flared in al-Dhabab, Hathran and Jabal Han as government troops have sought to thwart infiltration attempts and repel Houthi attacks. Sources within the government forces told Al Jazeera that troops captured 81 Houthi fighters in al-Dhabab on Monday afternoon.

In the southern and southwestern countryside, battles have intensified in the al-Shaqb, al-Aqroud and al-Misrakh areas. A field military source told Al Jazeera that government forces are involved in fierce clashes from all directions in the al-Shaqb area of Taiz, with confrontations extending to areas the Houthis seized on Monday in Sabir.

Also in the southwest, a field military source from the Southern Giants Brigades told Al Jazeera that Houthi forces had fired a ballistic missile at the highly strategic mountain range of Jabal Kahboub at midnight. The source confirmed there were no human or material casualties, with damage limited to the missile’s distant impact zone.

The military escalation has severely affected civilian populations. Al Jazeera correspondent Abdullah Qatran reported seeing Houthi mortar shelling targeting the al-Ikhwa residential neighbourhood in the centre of Taiz, resulting in an undetermined number of deaths, injuries and property damage, causing widespread panic.

With Taiz under Houthi siege, civilians there are also suffering severe shortages of fuel and other essential supplies. Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.

Compounding this, the Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms has documented 43 violations by Houthi forces in Taiz over the past 24 hours, which have killed five civilians and wounded 17. According to a report by Yemen’s state-run Saba news agency, casualties included five-year-old Ahlam Abdulsalam, who died when shelling struck her family’s home in the al-Misrakh district.

The rights group stated that Houthi forces have fired more than 180 projectiles at residential areas, including mortar and artillery shells, Katyusha rockets, tank rounds and drones. The bombardment has damaged seven homes, 12 private vehicles and the al-Saeed Mosque in Taiz city.

Saba also reported that a Houthi attack early on Tuesday struck al-Safwa Hospital, shattering windows, injuring at least one person, and triggering panic among patients and medical staff. This followed earlier Houthi shelling in which five people, including three children, were injured in the al-Dhahra residential area and the nearby Beer Basha district.

The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms warned that continuous shelling and restrictions on supplies are worsening humanitarian conditions, calling on the United Nations and the international community to take urgent steps to protect civilians.

articles.title: Xi’s trip to America was to boost his own image
articles.summary: He came, I think, not to engage the U.S. but to beam back to China televised images of Trump honoring him.
articles.body:
Xi Jinping was not interested in participating in meaningful discussions with President Trump when he visited Washington for the much-anticipated summit late last month. It is therefore time to stop intensive diplomacy with China.

In any event, the Chinese are not in the mood to deal constructively with anyone these days.

The substantive portion of the three-day meeting from Sept. 23-25 lasted less than two hours , so, after the subtraction of translation time, there was less than an hour of meaningful conversation. Xi, according to the Wall Street Journal , turned down an American request for a working lunch. There was, as a result, an unprecedented five-hour hole in the middle of the schedule on the 24th.

There was no joint statement afterwards. There were also significant differences in the post-summit readouts from Washington and Beijing . How could there be an agreement when there was so little time for conversation between the two leaders?

So, what did Xi come to America for? He came, I think, not to engage the U.S. but to beam back to China televised images of Trump honoring him.

“In the lead-up to the trip, Chinese officials are said to have contacted the embassies of other nations in Washington to compare notes and plan what one source called a ‘grand visit’ for Xi,” reported Hong Kong’s South China Morning Post. “A separate source said Beijing wanted to know what the Americans had done for other visiting foreign dignitaries, hoping to ‘take the best of all the different program options.’”

At the moment, the Chinese regime is not prepared to talk to those outside its border. As Charles Burton of the Prague-based think tank Sinopsis told me this month, “Beijing is buzzing these days as the Communist Party’s Central Committee is preparing for its Fifth Plenum.” The former Canadian diplomat in China pointed out that, “Traditionally, this plenum, which precedes a National Party Congress, is where leadership and succession groundwork is laid.” The politicking in the Communist Party is always intense, but now it is even more so.

It’s especially intense because Xi is not in good health, as evidenced by his shortened participation in last month’s BRICS summit — the coalition founded by Brazil, ​Russia, India and China — in New Delhi, and the light schedule in Washington. Xi’s frailty is partly responsible, I believe, for the signs of turbulence in senior Communist Party circles because potential successors are trying to position themselves for the top spot.

Despite his condition, Xi is reportedly demanding a fourth term as the Communist Party’s general secretary and, perhaps more importantly, as the party’s chairman of its Central Military Commission. At such a time, compromise with America is even less likely.

Chinese unwillingness to engage is also due to Xi’s perception of the long trend of events. He has, after all, staked his reputation on already surpassing America. His trademark phrase, introduced at the beginning of this decade, is “the East is rising and the West is declining” — and this makes it hard for him to compromise with what he maintains is a society on the wrong side of history.

No surprise then that at summits in May and September Xi mentioned the Thucydides Trap , his reference for a declining hegemon dangerously challenging a rising power.

Xi and Trump are scheduled to meet face-to-face twice more this year: once at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month and in Miami in December at the G20 summit. The prospects for progress this year are not good. As the Financial Times reports : “Beijing is focused on burnishing image while limiting dialogue.”

In these circumstances, why bother to meet in person? As a China watcher told me this month, “There is no longer a real need for ‘summits’ anyway, now that we have Zoom.” In fact, Chinese planners for the summit in Shenzhen want to move part of the event online , according to the Financial Times.

Dialogue is not important for China these days. Unfortunately, it has become an end in itself for America’s foreign policy establishment. The risk is that Washington’s obsessive pursuit of talking has only fed Xi’s already inflated sense of self-importance.

Moreover, as Washington officials talked over the course of decades, they created perverse incentives and tolerated China’s unacceptable behavior in the hope of convincing Chinese leaders to see things as they do.

Case in point: Beijing’s support for the Iranian war effort by providing satellite targeting data . This data almost certainly resulted in six American deaths on March 1, in Kuwait. After this, there must have been diplomacy behind the scenes. If so, the diplomacy obviously did not work: Chinese targeting data definitely resulted in three more American casualties on July 17, this time in Jordan.

(AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

articles.title: A little boy asked why his dad doesn't like him. His words broke my heart
articles.summary: Let me tell you about the hard work that we must do every day. Far too many of us make the mistake of trying to save young men only after they are broken.
articles.body: One of our young men came back from a day with the boys and told me he had to step away, so the child would not see him cry. The child, an 11-year-old with a buzzed head and a gap-tooth smile, told the young man that he loves coming around us because we feel like his uncles. Then the child got quiet. He said he gets sad sometimes because his dad never wants to talk to him or see him. What made the young man tear up was that the child then said that he hopes his father is doing good. "But why doesn’t my dad like me?" We all love this young boy and there is nothing not to like about him. He is good to his mother. He tries hard at school. He stands up to bullies and takes care of those around him. This boy is only 11. He is asking for guidance. He is asking for adults to guide him. If we don’t step up, the streets will take him. This is the hard work that we do every day. Far too many of us make the mistake of trying to save young men after they are broken. We hold the press conference after the shooting, myself included, and we say we must do better. We demand funding for programs after the arrest and the boy is long gone into the slammer. In the saddest cases, we write the obituary after the funeral and the family grieves over the senselessness. These tragedies happen because we often fail to build the boy before the streets define manhood for him. CHICAGO PASTOR GATHERS HUNDREDS OF MEN TO DECLARE VIOLENCE-FREE ZONE ON SOUTH SIDE By manhood I don’t mean puffing your chest like you're some bad dude. That’s an empty front. Manhood means discipline, responsibility, accountability, faith and all the qualities that allow one to stand strong on two feet. This boy is only 11. He is asking for guidance. He is asking for adults to guide him. If we don’t step up, the streets will take him. Every young boy learns from the men who stay and show how it is done. A young boy does not learn from a slogan, a speech or empty promises. The government can send a check, and it has sent more than its share into our neighborhood, but the government can never manufacture expectations. It cannot sit on the curb and talk to an 11-year-old boy who wants to know why his father disappeared. Last week, I stood in front of our new Leadership and Economic Opportunity Center that we built to steward young boys like our 11-year-old. High up on one of the window panes, someone shot a hole through the glass. This is the third window pane that has been broken. We’re talking thousands to repair the damage and we will replace them. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But think about what they shot. It wasn’t a liquor store or a vacant lot. It was a building — one of the first constructions on the South Side in who knows how long — going up where a motel notorious for crime once stood. And on a block that was known as America’s most dangerous. The government can send a check, and it has sent more than its share into our neighborhood, but the government can never manufacture expectations. It cannot sit on the curb and talk to an 11-year-old boy who wants to know why his father disappeared. This building houses job training facilities, classrooms, tutoring, violence prevention and so on. Most of all, this building was built to house young boys and girls who need the safety to grow into strong, resilient adults. Someone looked at all of that and fired a bullet at it. I’m ticked off and I'm upset. But I’m not quitting. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When that young man told me about that child and his father, I took that as a sign from God. I don’t know how, but I do know why and that is why I keep stepping forward. It is for these young boys. They need to see this building accomplished so they can understand what is expected of them in their lives. I know we cannot replace his father, but I know that we have no choice but to be vigilant with him and ensure that he grows up to be the father to his own son that he never had. articles.title: Palestinians dream of returning home after Israel raids West Bank camps
articles.summary: Palestinians have been displaced from their homes in Tulkarem refugee camp and dream of returning home.
articles.body:
Ramallah, occupied West Bank – Every day, Fuad Abu Salam sips his morning coffee outside his rented home in the Thinnabeh suburb, gazing at every detail of the sprawling Tulkarem refugee camp in front of him. This West Bank camp he can see in the distance once housed a two-storey building comprising four apartments, each measuring 300 square metres (3,229sq feet), in which he and his extended family lived.

After he was displaced from the camp, he, his wife, his four children, and his mother were confined to a small, rented apartment no bigger than 100sq metres (1,076sq feet) in Thinnabeh. His home in Tulkarem was partially destroyed when he left the camp.

Everything changed for Fuad and his family on January 21, 2025, when Israel launched a military assault in the occupied West Bank dubbed “Iron Wall”, initially targeting the Jenin refugee camp. A week later, the operation expanded to include the Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps in the city of Tulkarem.

Israeli forces forcibly displaced the entire populations of the three camps during January and February 2025 and continue to prevent their return, the United Nations has said.

Data from UNRWA cited in a report titled, Destruction of Palestinian Refugee Camps in the Northern West Bank, stated that 33,362 Palestinians remain forcibly displaced from the three camps. By October 2025, 52 percent of structures in the Jenin camp, 48 percent in the Nur Shams camp, and 36 percent in the Tulkarem camp had been destroyed or damaged.

The Israeli operation has affected hundreds of homes, roads, and infrastructure, including water and electricity networks, while humanitarian aid to the camps has been cut off.

Israeli forces killed 102 Palestinians, including 21 children, during the period covered, according to the report. This represents 46 percent of the total number of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank during this period.

On Sunday, the Israeli Supreme Court ordered the government to provide a timeline for the return of displaced people to the three camps, setting November 23 as a deadline for a response.

Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich rejected the ruling, warning that the return of residents could allow for the reconstruction of what he termed “terror infrastructure”. He called on the government not to implement the decision.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz opposed the court’s intervention, asserting that the army’s continued presence in the camps was a security decision and stating his intention to maintain a military presence there.

Fuad, 42, a greenhouse installer, found himself forced to flee with all the camp’s other residents and more than 40 family members. But he and his neighbours carried with them the hope of returning home.

They moved between the homes of relatives, enduring harsh living conditions, until he finally settled in the Thinnabeh suburb of Tulkarem.

The neighbourhood, which overlooks the camp, has “restored his spirit” because he can see his home even if it’s from afar. Although he is unable to reach the building, he can gaze at it and imagine a time when he can return.

“If a decision were issued right now allowing us to return, I would go back immediately without a moment’s hesitation,” he said.

But his home is no longer what it used to be. It was partially demolished and set on fire by Israeli soldiers, rendering more than 80 percent of the apartment block uninhabitable. Fuad plans to use the rubble to rebuild his home.

“I will never waver in my resolve to return, even if it means pitching a tent over the ruins and living there,” he declared.

Mohamad Ararawi, 18, from the Jenin refugee camp, also saw his home razed to the ground with a wide road replacing it.

He told Al Jazeera that his family of 40, who had lived in a five-story building in the al-Damaj neighbourhood, all fled the camp when the Israeli military operation began, seeking shelter in homes belonging to other relatives.

“My mother, father, five sisters, and I took refuge in my brother’s unfinished apartment. We endured harsh conditions, suffering through biting cold and scorching heat, before gradually completing the construction until it became somewhat habitable,” he added.

Returning is all that matters to them, and they refuse to live anywhere but the camp, even if it lacks basic amenities.

Returning the displaced back to their homes is not merely an issue of clearing roads for residents. Returning would mean living in a camp in which infrastructure has been damaged and hundreds of homes destroyed, all amid a lack of necessities.

Nihad Shawish, a member of the Nur Shams Camp Popular Services Committee, told Al Jazeera that the scale of destruction makes the residents’ return fraught with immense difficulties, despite their will to go back to their homes.

Approximately 400 homes, most of them three to four stories high, were destroyed, he said, while about 100 homes were burned down during the Israeli army’s presence in the camp.

Even the ones that survived are not necessarily habitable; they sustained severe damage affecting doors, windows, and interior facilities. The collapse of some buildings has also damaged neighbouring homes.

Approximately 10,900 camp residents remain displaced, including families staying in private homes and others at a school in the Thinnabeh suburb.

Faisal Salameh, an official with the Tulkarem Camp Popular Committee, told Al Jazeera that more than 2,000 housing units were completely destroyed, while approximately 90 per cent of the camp’s homes sustained partial damage, rendering them uninhabitable.

“Israel has turned the camp into an environment that drives residents away, given the widespread destruction and the ban on reconstruction in certain areas that have been converted into roads,” he noted.

Despite these conditions, Salameh said that displaced residents are eager to return to the camp as soon as a decision by the Israeli government permits them to.

The camp was home to approximately 15,000 people. The majority of the displaced currently live in rented homes or with relatives, while others have sought shelter in schools, mosques, or makeshift tin shacks.

While the Israeli Supreme Court’s ruling opens the door to discussing the return of displaced persons to camps in the northern West Bank, its rejection by Israeli government ministers raises questions about whether it will be implemented. Until then, the lives of the displaced families remain in limbo.

Mohamad Halaseh, an expert on Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that the Israeli right-wing isn’t just trying to alter the structure of the judicial system, but also seeking to undermine its legitimacy and exert pressure on judges.

He explained that the effect of political stances is evident in the disregard for Supreme Court rulings. He cites the issue of Palestinian prisoner visitations, a case in which the state failed to comply with the court’s decisions, as one example of this.

“The continued disregard for court rulings undermines the judiciary’s ability to compel the government to act when judicial decisions conflict with the stance of the political leadership,” he said.

Several precedents make the implementation of court rulings on the camps unlikely, he said. This is particularly distressing for residents who also face strong Israeli political opposition to the return of Palestinians to the three camps.

“Declared political stances set a limit on the extent to which executive institutions comply with judicial rulings,” he said.

articles.title: White House asks Guilfoyle to resign amid mounting scandals
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday the Trump administration has asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign. The news comes after President Trump told reporters Monday that he was considering firing Guilfoyle and that he was not happy with her amid snowballing scandals. The Wall Street Journal first reported last week…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday the Trump administration has asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign.

The news comes after President Trump told reporters Monday that he was considering firing Guilfoyle and that he was not happy with her amid snowballing scandals.

The Wall Street Journal first reported last week that Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 credit card bill and instructed him to do so via wire transfer to avoid a paper trail.

The Associated Press then reported Sunday that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were considering firing Guilfoyle.

Over the weekend, the Journal also reported that senior Trump administration officials were discussing the ambassador’s future in her post and that a decision from Trump would be coming shortly.

The outlet also reported new allegations that wealthy Greek businessmen helped fund Guilfoyle’s luxury travel as she used her role to promote their business interests.

Guilfoyle addressed her resignation in a statement on her personal social media X account, saying she rejected the allegations against her and would “vigorously” defend herself.

“I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service,” she wrote.

“While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end.”

Guilfoyle’s lawyers had earlier denied any wrongdoing. She reportedly is facing investigation by the State Department’s inspector general’s office.

As late as Tuesday, Guilfoyle was posting on social media about attending a diplomatic reception in her capacity as ambassador to Greece. The event marked Spain’s national day.

“The U.S. greatly values our deep transatlantic alliance and enduring partnership with Spain and Greece as we work together for regional peace and security,” Guilfoyle posted, alongside a photo with Spain’s ambassador to Greece .

Guilfoyle’s ousting does not, however, likely end scrutiny into her tenure as ambassador to Greece. The State Department’s inspector general launched an investigation into her conduct, the Daily Mail reported, looking into allegations of substance abuse, use of private planes and helicopters, close relationship with an energy and construction company, improper gift acceptance, and more.

It’s not clear if an investigation would cease after Guilfoyle’s departure, as the Office of Inspector General can use the report to make recommendations to the State Department to counter any potential wrongdoing in the future.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, issued a call on Sunday for the State OIG to investigate Guilfoyle. In a statement on X , Meeks said that “resigning does not shield her from accountability.”

“Guilfoyle used her position as a Trump official to get rich, while American families struggle with the cost of living,” he posted.

“Congress must conduct oversight to understand how this happened and hold the admin accountable.”

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), a rare Republican critic, welcomed the administration forcing Guilfoyle’s resignation. Curtis is homing in on corruption among Trump’s close circle, recently calling for an investigation into whether Donald Trump Jr.’s business ventures benefited from his father’s position and his ties to a Russian oligarch.

“I commend the Administration for taking the allegations involving Ambassador Guilfoyle seriously,” Curtis wrote in a statement on X .

“Public service is a public trust, and political connections should never put anyone above accountability. I appreciate President Trump’s willingness to act. That’s the kind of leadership Americans are yearning for.”

articles.title: Qantas plane grounded after reported bedbug outbreak
articles.summary: Passengers traveling from Italy to Australia failed to arrive in Perth as planned over the weekend, after their flight was canceled due to a reported case of bedbugs.
articles.body: Passengers traveling from Italy to Australia failed to arrive in Perth as planned over the weekend, after their flight was canceled due to a reported case of bedbugs. Qantas, Australian’s national airliner, was forced to cancel the flight scheduled for Saturday after passengers on an earlier incoming flight complained about being bitten onboard, according to CNN affiliate 9News. The Australian news outlet reported that complaints were made by travelers who had been in the economy section of flight QF5 from Perth to Rome the previous day, October 9. One of the passengers, Hailey Bagnall, told 9News: “(They were) crawling over our belongings, our clothing, our Qantas blankets, and they were even crawling along the window.” Qantas told CNN on Tuesday that it’s still investigating the incident, saying in a statement: “We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday’s Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue identified on a small number of economy seats.” The airline said that cabins are regularly cleaned to a high standard. Customers who had been due to fly on Saturday were provided with accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights, according to the airline. Bedbugs are small, flat insects. Reddish-brown in color, they tend to bite people while sleeping and feed on their blood, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). They can be found all over the world and in a variety of settings. Bites appear similar to those from mosquitoes and can appear swollen and itchy, with symptoms getting worse if the person is allergic to bedbugs. Contrary to what their name might suggest, they are not just found in beds. The CDC website states: “Bed bugs spread by getting into the seams and folds of luggage, overnight bags, folded clothes, bedding, furniture, and anywhere else they can hide. Most people do not realize they are transporting bed bugs and infecting areas as they travel. “ Bites do not usually require treatment beyond topical lotions. However, infested areas should be treated by pest control, the CDC says.

articles.title: How the midterms could impact US-Mexico relations
articles.summary: The midterms could give Mexico more allies in Washington who value a stable North American partnership.
articles.body:
Mexico is paying close attention to the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. A change in control of Congress would not put a Democrat in the White House or end the pressures on Mexico over trade, migration and security. It would, however, change who can demand answers, control hearings and shape the terms of any lasting agreement. For a country accustomed to dealing directly with the U.S. executive branch, that would be a consequential shift.

Democrats have a plausible path to the House, while the Senate remains uncertain . A Democratic House could summon officials, investigate decisions and write spending bills. A Senate victory would give the party more leverage over legislation and appointments. The White House would still direct U.S. negotiations through January 2029, even as the next presidential race begins to shape political incentives.

The first test will be the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement . At the July joint review, Washington declined to extend the agreement in its current form. The agreement remains in force, with annual reviews ahead unless the three governments agree to extend it.

Meanwhile, the U.S. and Mexican governments are trying to reach a bilateral understanding before the election. Mexico wants relief from U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles; Washington is pressing for changes that benefit American producers and narrow its trade deficit.

An announcement before November could resolve some disputes but would leave essential questions unanswered. Would Canada be brought back into a durable trilateral arrangement? Which concessions can the White House deliver, and which changes would require Congress to amend U.S. law? Those questions would land on Capitol Hill in January.

The House Ways and Means Committee would be the place to start. Its Democrats regard the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement as a source of stability and have criticized the administration’s use of tariffs against close partners. If their party wins the House, expect closer scrutiny of the negotiations and a stronger insistence on consultation.

But Mexico should not mistake that for an invitation to relax. Ways and Means Democrats want tougher labor and environmental enforcement as well as secure supply chains. Across the aisle, Republicans have pressed Mexico over energy policies and loopholes that allow goods from outside North America to claim regional benefits.

The Senate Finance Committee would matter just as much for any major trade legislation. A proposal from its Democratic side would restore more congressional authority over tariffs and binding trade agreements.

Whether or not Democrats win the Senate, there is a constituency in Congress for a trade relationship that gives businesses greater predictability while demanding that Mexico fulfill its commitments. A divided Congress could make a wholesale rewrite harder, but oversight of the existing agreement could grow more intense.

Money is the next lever. House Appropriations would influence funding for customs facilities, border inspection, anti-fentanyl efforts and cooperation between agencies. Its Homeland Security subcommittee brings the interests of border communities into decisions about staffing, inspection technology and the movement of legitimate commerce.

A Democratic House could write different priorities into spending bills, although the Senate and president would still have to agree to enact them. That makes bipartisan support for practical border improvements essential.

Security policy could produce the sharpest public disagreements. A Democratic House Homeland Security Committee would be more likely to question how the administration conducts immigration enforcement and works with Mexico against fentanyl trafficking. House Foreign Affairs, including its Western Hemisphere subcommittee, would scrutinize the diplomatic consequences of threats to use force inside Mexico.

House Democrats have already warned against unilateral military action without Mexico’s consent and congressional authorization. That stance does not mean less interest in stopping fentanyl. It points toward a fight over methods, sovereignty and whether cooperation is producing results.

There is, however, one area where a change of majority may alter the language more than the underlying demand: China.

Both parties worry about Chinese investment and inputs entering North American supply chains through Mexico. The House committee focused on China would continue to press questions about ownership, traceability and strategic materials if the next House renews its mandate. The U.S. and Mexico have already announced a critical minerals action plan . Mexico will be judged on whether it can turn that cooperation into credible rules, processing capacity and reliable infrastructure.

Energy poses another test. Republicans emphasize market access for U.S. investors, while Democrats may emphasize environmental standards and clean power. Both will ask whether Mexico can supply reliable electricity to sustain North American manufacturing.

Mexico, therefore, needs a strategy for Congress as well as the White House. That means engaging trade and spending committees, members from manufacturing and border states, labor and business groups and governors whose economies depend on cross-border production.

It also means arriving with evidence: measurable progress at customs, credible action against criminal networks, enforceable labor commitments and a convincing plan to supply the energy and water that new industry requires.

The midterms could give Mexico more allies in Washington who value a stable North American partnership. They could also give its critics more platforms from which to demand change. Mexico should prepare to answer to more of Washington, more often and in public.

Duncan Wood, Ph.D. is CEO of Hurst International Consulting and a fellow at the Wilson Center. Ivan Zapien is a partner in Global Regulatory Affairs at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader.
